question: Can you get up off the floor without your hands?

say: You treat the floor like lava now: down is easy, but up needs a hand, a knee, and a small prayer to the sofa.
You have not lost a party trick. You have lost a basic move.
Your body was built to sit on the floor and stand back up in one piece, using strength, balance and flexibility together.
Researchers scored exactly that move in two thousand and two adults who sat on the floor and rose again.
Every hand or knee cost a point, and low scores were linked to higher death rates afterwards.
Each extra point was linked to a twenty one percent improvement in survival.
So win the points back beside a sturdy chair: its seat first, then one hand, then a fingertip, then nothing.
Train the parts twice a week: chair stands, calf raises, and slow trips down to the floor and back.
Plain warning: if you have fallen, hurt your head, back, neck or hip, or you cannot get up, call for emergency help and keep warm while you wait.
If you have not exercised for a while, talk to your doctor first.
Let's get you back to factory settings.

brito2014: de Brito LBB, Ricardo DR, Araujo DSMS, Ramos PS, Myers J, Araujo CGS. Ability to sit and rise from the floor as a predictor of all-cause mortality. Eur J Prev Cardiol 2014;21(7):892 to 898 (PubMed abstract, PMID 23242910): the test group is described as "2002 adults aged 51-80 years (68% men) performed a sitting-rising test (SRT) to and from the floor", one point was subtracted for each support used (hand or knee), and the lowest scoring group had the highest adjusted hazard ratio. Survival finding, quoted: "Each unit increase in SRT score conferred a 21% improvement in survival." The test is described as "influenced by muscular strength and flexibility". Retrospective cohort, median follow up 6.3 years, so the script says linked to, not caused by.
cdc: CDC, Preventing Falls and Hip Fractures, Older Adult Fall Prevention (page dated Jan 27, 2026, opened 13 Oct 2026): under Do strength and balance exercises, quoted: "Do exercises that make your legs stronger and improve your balance." The same page tells readers to ask their doctor to evaluate their risk of falling.
nhsfalls: NHS, Falls (page last reviewed 06 March 2025, opened 13 Oct 2026): after a fall, quoted in part: "Take a couple of minutes to check for any pain or injuries". The same page says to call 999 if someone who has fallen may have injured the head, back, neck or hip, or cannot get up; if you feel able to get up, roll onto your side, push up onto hands and knees, look for something stable to hold such as heavy furniture, put one foot flat on the floor and stand up slowly; if you cannot get up, get help, keep warm, keep moving, and change position about every 30 minutes.
nhsguide: NHS, Physical activity guidelines for older adults (opened 13 Oct 2026): adults aged 65 and over should "do activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week" and "Speak to a GP first if you have not exercised for some time". The script's twice a week training line and its talk to your doctor line rest on this page.
nhsinform: NHS Inform (NHS Scotland), Strength and balance exercises (opened 13 Oct 2026): sit to stand section, quoted in part: "Moving from sitting to standing is a core exercise that will help to improve your strength and balance." and "make sure you've got a solid chair." The same page sets out a handhold ladder for the exercise: push firmly on the arms of the chair, then a light fingertip touch, then fold your arms and let your legs do the work; it also lists calf or heel raises, and says to start holding on and reduce the handhold over time.
